chapter: Funerals, Mardi Gras and civil rights
title: Mardi Gras as a child and playing it as a young musician
summary: Neutral-ground Mardi Gras, the Zulu float page in 1940, and the black float builder at Corpus Christi School.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: People often talk about Mardi Gras and Mardi Gras celebration. What did you do on Mardi Gras? Was Mardi Gras special when you were growing up, when you were a kid?

When I was a kid, Mardi Gras was very, oh yeah, it was a good time, you know. I can't remember. I can't remember. Okay, I can remember when I was first Mardi Gras parade. But otherwise, Mardi Gras day was the day that we went and played at this place or that place. As a young musician I'm talking about now. We played like the hi-hat, the San Jacinto, or the Blue Eagle uptown. Different places, you know. And in the daytime, there was always some place that people might have hired you to play for a couple of hours in front of their ballroom or something like that, you know. That's the way it was when I was younger. Now, after I played my first parade with George Williams in 1958 or 9 or whatever it was, then from then on it was parades every year up until.
I'm thinking more when you were five, six, seven years old with the family. Did the family do anything together in Mardi Gras?

Not that I can remember except for Clayborne Street was like only a half a block away. And it was a neutral ground that the black people lined up and they had sandwiches and stuff. And we would wait to see the Indians or the skeletons or the baby doll. So either somebody dressed in a pair of Union drawers with a yellow mustard running down the back of them or something like that. That's what I can remember as a young, about six, I would say six and seven years old. Four or five, I don't know what I did.
Now, did you dress up as a kid? What did you do?
Um, I don't believe. I don't believe. No, I didn't. I had more, when it became time that I may have dressed up, I was into music.
But if they dressed me up as a little guy, five, six years old, I can't remember.
But I don't think it was that serious.
You ought to know if your parents were part of like an organization that dressed up on carnival.

My parents had a friend because in 1940, oh, I'll tell you what, I was a page on a float in 1940 with King Zulu. His name was Manuel Bernard. And he was my daddy's best friend. And I was a page. And you know, another thing is, when I went to school at Copa's Christie, there was always, we didn't worry so much about Mardi Gras, but there was the Kitty's Day Parade. And there was a man, and his name was Lawrence, Lawrence Toka, not Lawrence Toka, Merkendale. Lawrence Merkendale was one of the first float builders of this city. He was a black man. Mm-hmm. And he built floats for Copa's Christie School because we had a pageant every year around early spring called the Kitty's Day Parade. And he made these floats out of old bottom of automobiles, which he stretched and put wheels on and so forth. And after school, us kids would help him to paint these floats. He made it out of cardboard and paper mache. In those days, it was like wedding newspaper and putting it on wire and all kind of stuff. He was very smart at that.
